setup: Before the story of Peter and his heirs begins, you need the machine they all ran, because the whole book is an argument about it. In 1914 the Russian Empire covered about 8.6 million square miles, a sixth of all the land on the planet, more than twice the size of the United States including Alaska, and governing something that size with the technology of 1700 or 1800 is the central engineering problem of everything that follows. The state's answer had three load-bearing parts. Autocracy: rule by one tsar answerable to no law and no parliament, where any limit on his will was treated as a kind of blasphemy. Orthodoxy: a church that, after Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, styled Moscow the Third Rome and served as an arm of the throne rather than a check on it. And serfdom: by the 1649 Ulozhenie, somewhere around 23 million people, more than a third of the population, were owned, bought, sold, and flogged. What is at stake across this book is whether you can keep the grandeur at the top while never surrendering the unfreedom at the bottom, and the state's two-century wager that you could.

bridge: Chapter 1 laid out the machine Peter is about to inherit: an autocratic tsar, a church that served the throne, and 23 million serfs bound to the land by the 1649 law code. The state he gets is not yet the Russian Empire but Muscovy, large, cold, landlocked, and by the standard of the Dutch or the Swedes a century behind, with no warm-water port, almost no navy, and a half-medieval army. The three load-bearing parts are all in place. What is missing is the grandeur. The boy who will supply it, with a brutality few rulers in any country match, is about to be marked for life by the violence of the very soldiers who guard the capital.
setup: Pyotr Alekseyevich Romanov is born on 9 June 1672, the first child of Tsar Alexei's second wife. He is bright and healthy; his older half-brother Ivan is half-blind and, the sources say, intellectually disabled. With no ironclad rule of succession, the crown becomes a faction fight between two clans, the Naryshkins behind Peter and the Miloslavskys behind Ivan, and the faction that controls the capital's soldiers wins. In May 1682 the streltsy storm the Kremlin, and the nine-year-old Peter watches men he knows torn apart on their pikes. Out of that comes a dual monarchy, both boys crowned, real power going to their half-sister Sophia as regent, the first woman to rule Russia in her own right. Shunted off to a village to be neutralized, Peter instead raises his own play regiments, falls in with the foreigners of the German Quarter, and teaches himself shipbuilding and the West. Whether this traumatized, self-taught outsider can outlast Sophia and seize his own throne is what this chapter settles.

cast.note: the nine-year-old who watches the massacre, future Peter the Great

cast.name: Sophia Alekseyevna
cast.note: half-sister and regent, first woman to rule Russia outright

cast.name: Ivan V

takeaway: By the end you'll understand the trauma that made Peter hate Moscow, and how a boy raised on play soldiers and a leaky boat came to rule a continent.

bridge: Chapter 2 left Peter, at twenty-four, ruling alone after outlasting his half-sister Sophia and the death of co-tsar Ivan. He has a country the size of a continent and almost nothing a great power needs: no warm-water port, no real navy, a half-medieval army. His first reach for the sea, the Azov campaigns, taught him two lessons that organize everything now, that sea power was not optional and that to get it he needed western knowledge, western specialists, and western money, and that he would have to go and see for himself. In 1697 the tsar of Russia leaves his own country in disguise to learn a trade.
setup: The Grand Embassy of about 250 people sets out for the West, and Peter travels incognito as carpenter Peter Mikhailov so he can skip the ceremony and work a shipyard with his own hands. He labors in the Dutch yards, tours the Royal Society and the Mint where Newton was Warden, looks in on a Parliament England had since 1265 and Russia would not get for two centuries, and ships home hundreds of foreign experts. Then comes the war that makes the empire. Russia is sealed off from the Baltic by Sweden, in 1700 the dominant military power of northern Europe under the teenage prodigy Charles XII. Peter declares war and is humiliated at Narva in 1700, but Charles turns away to deal with Poland and leaves him six years to rebuild the army from the ground up. In the middle of the war, in 1703, Peter founds St Petersburg on a frozen swamp, his window to Europe, raised by conscripted labor on a scale the death toll has made proverbial. Whether this transformed Russia can break Sweden and force a window onto the sea is the chapter's question.

takeaway: By the end you'll understand how a man who learned to caulk a hull won the Baltic at Poltava and turned Muscovy into the Russian Empire.

bridge: Across the last two chapters Peter dragged a half-medieval Muscovy onto the sea: he toured the West in disguise to learn its technique, rebuilt the army, beat Sweden's Charles XII at Poltava in 1709, raised St Petersburg on a swamp, and in 1721 took the Baltic coast by the Treaty of Nystad and the title Emperor of All Russia. The grandeur was now undeniable, a navy, a European-drilled army, a half-built western capital. This chapter is the bill for it: the machinery Peter built to run a modern state, and the people that machinery ran over, because both halves are the thesis.
setup: Peter is above all an institution-builder. He replaces the old tangle of departments with a rationalized state copied from Sweden, a Governing Senate, functional Colleges, a surveillance corps to watch the officials. His Table of Ranks of 1722 makes status flow from service to the state, converting the hereditary nobility into a service class that owes its privileges, above all the right to own serfs, to the crown. The soul tax fixes every peasant in place as a permanent tax-unit, deepening serfdom in the act of funding the empire. The culture war lands as an assault on the soul of Orthodox Russia: the beard tax, Western dress, and above all the decapitation of the church, the Patriarchate left vacant from 1700 and abolished in 1721, replaced by a Holy Synod run by a lay official. To his enemies and the persecuted Old Believers, Peter is literally the Antichrist. The question this chapter sets up is what the forced grandeur cost, and who paid, including a son.

takeaway: By the end you'll see how Peter clamped a modern state onto a society that grew none of it, leaving no heir and a throne for the Guards to decide.

bridge: Peter the Great died in February 1725 having built a modern state by force and broken the old rule of succession without replacing it. In 1722 he had a law passed letting the emperor name any heir he chose, and then died naming no one, after having his own son tortured to death for opposing the reforms. The throne of the largest empire on earth was now an open question, and the only institution in the capital with both the weapons and the proximity to settle it was the Guards, the play regiments Peter had raised as a boy. For the next thirty-seven years, that is how Russia chooses its rulers.
setup: This is the age when Russian successions are settled at three in the morning by whichever faction the Preobrazhensky and Semyonovsky regiments back. A parade of rulers passes: Peter's servant-born widow Catherine I, the boy Peter II, then Anna, who in 1730 is offered the throne only if she signs written Conditions limiting her power, signs them, then tears them up to a roar of approval from the Guards, the autocracy's clearest near-death before 1905. The infant Ivan VI is deposed and vanishes into secret confinement; Elizabeth seizes power in 1741 by personally leading the grenadiers from their barracks. Underneath the coups, two things grow: the top-down knowledge machine starts producing Russians, like the fisherman's son Lomonosov, not just importing Germans, and Rastrelli gives imperial grandeur its definitive look in palaces raised by a serf economy. The age ends with Peter III, a six-month emperor who frees the nobility from compulsory service while leaving the serf bound, the exact structural injustice the next 155 years gnaw on.

takeaway: By the end you'll see the autocracy's hidden dependency, an absolute ruler chosen by a few thousand soldiers, and the moral crack the whole edifice eventually falls into.

bridge: Chapter 5 ended with Peter III, the six-month emperor whose one lasting act was to free the nobility from compulsory service while leaving the serf bound. He was personally unpopular, contemptuous of Russian feeling, and within months overthrown and killed by a conspiracy fronted by the Guards and led by his own wife, a minor German princess who had spent eighteen years quietly preparing for exactly this. Her name was Catherine, and the next four chapters are hers. She takes the throne as a usurper with no Russian blood and no hereditary right at all, while the actual Romanov heir, her son Paul, is alive and a child.
setup: She was born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst in 1729 and becomes Catherine the Great, the most formidable ruler Russia has between Peter and the twentieth century, and the chapter where the book's central contradiction stops being a diagram and becomes one person's biography. She believed, sincerely and at length, in the European Enlightenment's program of reason, law, and human dignity, and she ruled a state that ran on the opposite of all three, and she knew it, and she chose the state. She corresponds with Voltaire, buys Diderot's library, founds the Hermitage, has herself publicly inoculated against smallpox in 1768. She personally writes the Nakaz, lifted from Montesquieu and Beccaria, and convenes a Legislative Commission of 564 deputies, pointedly excluding the serfs, to make a new law code. Whether the philosopher-empress will touch serfdom, when her throne rests on the support of the serf-owning nobility that made her and can unmake her, is the chapter's hinge.

cast.name: Catherine the Great
cast.note: German-born usurper, the dynasty's most intelligent ruler

cast.name: Voltaire
cast.note: Europe's most famous writer, her decades-long correspondent

cast.name: The Orlov brothers
cast.note: Guards officers who organized her 1762 coup

cast.name: Joseph II
cast.note: the Habsburg rival who abolished serfdom; her counter-example

takeaway: By the end you'll understand why the most enlightened ruler the dynasty produced concluded she could free her mind on paper but never the serf.

bridge: In Chapter 6, Catherine the Great intellectually conceded the case against serfdom in the privacy of her Nakaz, convened a Legislative Commission that produced no law, and concluded, correctly for holding power, that she could not touch the bondage her throne rested on. She had reasoned her way to a limit. This chapter is where that limit is demonstrated to her from below, in blood, by 23 million people's answer to the question her Commission refused to ask.
setup: First the book makes you stand inside serfdom in concrete human terms. A privately owned serf around 1770 could be bought, sold, advertised in newspapers, flogged, exiled to Siberia, and by a 1767 decree sentenced to hard labor merely for petitioning against his master; roughly 23 million of them, a bound population larger than all of Britain, were held in the villages that fed the capital. Then add the frontier: the Cossacks, free militarized communities whose autonomy Catherine's centralizing state was eroding, smoldering with fury. The spark is the classic Russian one, the pretender. Yemelyan Pugachev, a Don Cossack deserter, declares in 1773 that he is the murdered Peter III returned to free the people, and his rebellion of 1773-1775 becomes the largest popular uprising before the twentieth century, raising armies tens of thousands strong and burning Kazan. The chapter's whole argument is what the terror does to Catherine, and it is the opposite of mercy: she moves hard the other way, toward the Charter to the Nobility that makes the chain tighter than Peter ever did.

cast.note: Cossack deserter posing as the returned Peter III

cast.name: Catherine the Great
cast.note: the philosopher-empress who answers revolt with repression

cast.name: The Cossacks
cast.note: free frontiersmen whose eroded autonomy fed the revolt

cast.name: Alexander Radishchev
cast.note: first noble to indict serfdom in print, called worse than Pugachev

takeaway: By the end you'll understand why the great revolt moved the regime not toward freedom but toward locking the chain harder, and why every later revolutionary is an echo of Pugachev.

bridge: While Catherine the Great was tightening the chain at home after Pugachev (Chapter 7), she was expanding the empire faster than any Russian ruler since Peter. This chapter follows the other hand, the conquering one, and carries a second face of the thesis: grandeur in the Russian system meant not only palaces and the Hermitage but land, and the conversion of conquered peoples into subjects of the autocracy who never consented. By the time Catherine died in 1796 she had added some 200,000 square miles and seven million people and wiped a thousand-year-old European country off the map.
setup: Start in the south, where the grandeur was loudest. Catherine fights two long wars against the Ottoman Empire and wins both: a fleet sails the length of Europe to burn the Turks at Chesma in 1770, the 1774 Treaty of Kuchuk-Kainarji wins a Black Sea navy and a claim to protect Ottoman Christians that will light the Crimean War, and in 1783 she annexes Crimea outright. Her partner Potemkin builds the new south of Novorossiya, founding cities including Odessa and giving history the durable, largely false myth of the Potemkin villages. Then the cold part: in three Partitions in 1772, 1793, and 1795, Russia, Prussia, and Austria erase the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the largest state in Europe, off the map for 123 years despite Kosciuszko's 1794 uprising, absorbing millions of Poles, Catholics, and Jews who become a permanent grievance. And in the opposite direction, almost as an afterthought, fur traders found the first settlements of Russian America, reaching down the Pacific coast toward California. Every conquest, the chapter argues, made the empire larger and harder to hold in the same act.

cast.name: Catherine the Great
cast.note: doubles the empire while refusing to free a single serf

cast.name: Grigory Potemkin
cast.note: built the conquered south, namesake of the village myth

cast.name: Alexander Suvorov
cast.note: the general who never lost a battle, stormed Izmail in 1790

cast.name: Tadeusz Kosciuszko

takeaway: By the end you'll see imperial grandeur measured in square miles and in the erasure of a sovereign nation, each conquest making the empire bigger and weaker at once.

bridge: Catherine the Great died in 1796 having doubled the empire abroad and locked serfdom tighter at home, and the throne passed to the one person she had least wanted to have it: her son Paul, whom she had sidelined for thirty-four years and was widely believed to have wanted to skip over entirely. Paul grew up the rightful heir, watching, embittered, half-convinced his mother had murdered his father Peter III and stolen his crown. He becomes emperor at forty-two and rules like a man settling scores.
setup: Paul I reigns only five years and is genuinely contradictory, so the label "the mad tsar" needs handling with care. He does one thing of permanent importance, the 1797 Pauline Law of Succession that abolishes Peter's disastrous name-any-heir rule and fixes strict male primogeniture, ending the disputed successions and Guards-made emperors for good. But he persecutes the nobility, lurches in foreign policy, and in March 1801 is strangled in his bedroom by a conspiracy of officers, the last successful palace coup in Russian history. His son and heir, Alexander, was in the palace that night and had given conditional blessing to his father's removal on the promise that Paul would only be made to abdicate. He begins his reign as a guilt-shadowed probable accomplice to the murder, soaked by his tutor in Enlightenment ideals, privately discussing a constitution and the end of serfdom with his young friends, and backing the reform plans of the priest's-son genius Speransky. Whether any of it can survive the load-bearing wall of the regime, and the gathering storm of Napoleon, is the question.

cast.note: embittered son who fixed the succession, then was murdered

cast.name: Alexander I
cast.note: guilt-shadowed reformer-tsar, probable accomplice to the murder

cast.name: Mikhail Speransky

cast.name: Napoleon

takeaway: By the end you'll see the reform pattern repeat once more, drafted, half-believed, stopped by the regime's wall, just as the largest invasion army in history crosses the border.

bridge: Chapter 9 left Alexander I as a haunted, guilt-ridden emperor who had dreamed of constitutions, exiled his reformer Speransky to noble pressure on the eve of war, and still owned 23 million serfs. His decade of wars had gone badly, beaten by Napoleon at Austerlitz in 1805 and Friedland in 1807, forced into the humiliating Treaty of Tilsit on a raft in the Niemen and into a blockade of Britain that wrecked Russian trade. The alliance was hollow from the first day. Both emperors prepared for the war they knew was coming, and in June 1812 the largest invasion army in history crosses the border heading east.
setup: Napoleon Bonaparte crosses the Niemen with the Grande Armee, on the order of 600,000 men, the largest army Europe had ever assembled. He does not want to hold Russia; he wants one fast crushing battle to force Alexander back to heel. The Russian commanders do the one thing that defeats his method, refusing the decisive battle and retreating deep into the enormous country, trading the empire's vast space for time and burning supplies behind them, the same strategy that beat Charles XII at Poltava. Public fury at the retreat forces Alexander to hand command to the old, fatalistic Kutuzov, who must give Russia a battle. He gives it at Borodino on 7 September 1812, one of the bloodiest single days before the twentieth century, then chooses to abandon Moscow, judging that losing Moscow was not losing Russia but losing the army would be. Moscow burns, Napoleon sits in the ashes, and the retreat becomes the catastrophe. This is the most mythologized episode in the book, so the chapter keeps flagging which famous parts are solid and which are the legend doing its work.

cast.note: invader whose Grande Armee distance and winter destroy

cast.name: Mikhail Kutuzov
cast.note: one-eyed fatalist who trades Moscow to save the army

cast.name: Barclay de Tolly
cast.note: war minister who began the deep scorched-earth retreat

takeaway: By the end you'll understand how the empire's impossible size became its weapon for once, and why the summit of its grandeur is reached without changing a thing inside it.

bridge: Chapter 10 ended at the summit of Russia's grandeur: Napoleon's Grande Armee destroyed by space, hunger, and cold, Russia the dominant land power of Europe, and Alexander I riding through Paris as the most powerful monarch in the world, the principal author of Napoleon's downfall. And the empire had done it all without changing a single thing inside itself. The serf who marched to Paris and saw a Europe without serfdom came home in 1815 to a village where he was still owned. Some of those soldiers, and the young officers who led them, brought the contradiction back across the border and could not put it down.
setup: For ten years after 1815 Russia is the most powerful state in the world, and it uses that power almost entirely to prevent change anywhere. At the Congress of Vienna, Alexander I is the dominant figure; he gains Congress Poland and, in a move that captures his lifelong contradiction, grants it a written constitution and an elected Sejm while his own empire has neither. He proposes the Holy Alliance, which becomes the flag of the conservative order and makes Russia the gendarme of Europe, the continent's cop, ready to march and crush a revolution anywhere. At home the reaction takes a grotesque form in Arakcheyev's military colonies, whole districts of peasants regimented as permanent army settlements. Then comes the morning the book has been walking toward. Alexander dies suddenly in 1825, a confused three-week succession leaves it unclear who the emperor is, and into that gap step the Decembrists, aristocratic officers who had marched to Paris and read the liberalism their own emperor suppressed. The question is what happens when the empire's own elite brings the grandeur and the unfreedom into open, armed collision for the first time.

cast.note: Europe's arbiter and the continent's conservative gendarme

cast.name: The Decembrists
cast.note: aristocratic officers demanding a constitution and freed serfs

cast.name: Nicholas I
cast.note: the new tsar who answers the revolt with grapeshot

cast.name: Count Arakcheyev

takeaway: By the end you'll understand why a revolt that failed in a single afternoon changed everything afterward, the moment the long fuse was lit and the torch passed.

bridge: Chapter 11 ended on the morning of 14 December 1825, when aristocratic officers, the Decembrists, refused the oath to a new tsar and assembled under arms demanding a constitution and an end to serfdom. The revolt failed in a single afternoon when Nicholas I, on his first day as emperor, fired grapeshot into Senate Square; five ringleaders were hanged and over a hundred exiled to Siberia. It changed nothing in 1825 and everything afterward, lighting the long fuse. Nicholas's entire reign becomes one long attempt to stamp it out.
setup: Nicholas I becomes tsar ordering grapeshot fired at the Decembrists and spends thirty years making sure that morning never happens again. His education minister formulates the regime's first explicit doctrine, Official Nationality, the triad Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality, an argument that Russia is strong precisely because it has not become Europe. To enforce it Nicholas builds the Third Section, the empire's first centralized political police, the direct ancestor of the Okhrana and the Soviet security organs; he crushes the Polish November Uprising of 1830-1831 and abolishes Poland's constitution. And here is the paradox: the most repressive reign of the century is the foundational age of Russian literature, because when every other avenue of public life is closed, the novel becomes the only place a thinking Russian can examine the country. Pushkin, who created the modern literary language, dies in a duel in 1837; Gogol's Dead Souls satirizes a society that literally trades human beings; the intelligentsia is born and splits into Westernizers and Slavophiles. The chapter closes with the 1849 mock execution of the Petrashevsky Circle, twenty-one men including the young Dostoevsky marched before a firing squad to teach the country the price of thought.

cast.name: Sergei Uvarov

takeaway: By the end you'll see how total repression bred a national literature, and how the intelligentsia that would destroy the autocracy was born inside its most controlled reign.

bridge: Chapter 12 left Nicholas I at the apogee of autocracy: the Third Section watching everything, the press silenced, the Petrashevsky men marched to a fake execution, the most thoroughly controlled state in Europe. For forty years since 1815, Russia had been the gendarme of Europe, the showcase of Official Nationality, the proof, the regime believed, that autocracy and unfreedom produced strength. It looked, from the inside, like total success. The Crimean War is the experiment that tests that claim against reality, in public, on Russian soil.
setup: The Crimean War of 1853-1856 is the shortest era the book gives a whole chapter, because its meaning is single and overwhelming. Nicholas I inflates a quarrel over the holy sites in Jerusalem into a confrontation with the Ottomans, misjudging that Britain, France, and Austria would not let him dismember them; instead he ends up isolated, the gendarme of Europe with no friends in Europe. The fighting comes to Russia's own Crimea, to the siege of Sevastopol, which holds for nearly a year. The Russian defense is, in individual courage, magnificent, the surgeon Pirogov pioneering battlefield triage, the young artillery officer Leo Tolstoy writing his Sevastopol Sketches. But the system behind the courage loses, because Russia, fighting on its own soil, cannot supply its own army while Britain and France project power across a continent by railway and steamship. Russia had almost no railways and moved troops by ox-cart, specifically behind the industrial-policy states it had watched modernize for two decades. Nicholas dies in February 1855, a broken man, before Sevastopol falls. The question is what the audit reveals, and what it costs the regime to learn it.

cast.note: the tsar whose doctrine of strength the war refutes

cast.name: Leo Tolstoy

cast.name: Nikolai Pirogov

takeaway: By the end you'll understand how a war fought on home ground killed not just a quarter-million Russians but the regime's central belief that unfreedom made it strong.

bridge: The Crimean War (Chapter 13) returned its unanswerable verdict: the system as it stood could not defend the country, and Nicholas I died a broken man watching it fail. His son Alexander II inherited the losing war, ended it on humiliating terms, and faced the same collision every reforming ruler in this book had faced, the choice between the grandeur and the unfreedom. Unlike Catherine and Alexander I before him, he is about to become the one autocrat who chooses, on the central question, to give up the unfreedom.
setup: Alexander II tells the reluctant Moscow nobility in 1856 that it is better to abolish serfdom from above than wait for it to abolish itself from below, framing the reform not as conscience but as regime self-preservation against a national Pugachev. The Emancipation of the Serfs of 19 February 1861 frees around 23 million privately owned serfs, the single largest act of legislative liberation in history to that point, peacefully, two years before Lincoln's Proclamation and without the war that killed 750,000 Americans. But the mechanism sabotages the act: freed peasants get less land than they farmed, owe forty-nine years of redemption payments, and are bound to the village commune, the mir. The chain is not struck off but re-forged in a new shape. The disappointment is so deep it becomes an engine of revolution. The Great Reforms follow, the elected zemstvo councils, independent courts with jury trial, universal military service, and they are the genuine article, but every one of them stops at the same wall: Alexander II refuses, flatly, every request for a national parliament. The question is what that mismatch, a modernized body under an untouched autocratic head, eventually detonates.

cast.note: the Tsar Liberator who frees the serfs but won't share power

cast.note: 23 million given liberty but bound to debt and the commune

cast.name: The mir

bridge: Chapter 14 freed the serfs in 1861 but cheated them, less land than they farmed, decades of redemption debt, and binding to the commune, while Alexander II refused every request for a national parliament. The disappointment convinced a generation of educated young Russians that the autocracy was structurally incapable of giving real freedom and would have to be destroyed, not petitioned. This chapter carries the fuse, lit by the Decembrists and passed through the literature of Nicholas's reign, to the people who spend the next four decades trying to blow up the empire.
setup: A new psychological type appears, the raznochintsy, poorer and harder than the aristocratic thinkers of the 1840s, contemptuous of inherited authority. Turgenev's 1862 Fathers and Sons gives the world the word nihilist; Chernyshevsky's What Is to Be Done?, written in a prison cell, becomes the radicals' bible. They try three strategies in sequence. First propaganda: in 1874 thousands of students go to the people in the countryside, and the devout, monarchist peasants often tie up the agitators and march them to the police. Then, after that failure, Land and Liberty splits in 1879, and the larger faction, the People's Will, adopts systematic political assassination as a theorized program, the ancestors of much of modern terrorism. They sentence the emperor to death and spend two years hunting him, smuggling dynamite into the Winter Palace itself. On the morning of 1 March 1881 Alexander II approves the modest Loris-Melikov step toward representation; that afternoon a second bomber kills him. The question is what his murder produces, and the answer is not the revolution they expected.

cast.name: The People's Will
cast.note: the group that pioneers systematic political assassination

cast.name: Alexander II
cast.note: the Tsar Liberator hunted and killed by those he freed

bridge: The chapters around this one are about the empire hunting and being hunted, the People's Will killing Alexander II in 1881 and the reaction that followed. This chapter breaks the chronology on purpose, because its subject does not fit on a timeline. Across roughly the second half of the nineteenth century, the same empire that flogged peasants and hanged students produced what is, by wide agreement, the single greatest concentration of literature any country has produced in a comparable span, plus world-altering music and science, and it did so while the autocracy held and the unfreedom only half-lifted.
setup: This is the thesis at its most uncomfortable, because the grandeur here is not palaces or conquests, easy to see through, but War and Peace and the periodic table, achievements of permanent value to all humanity, made by the same machine. The argument the book has built since Chapter 12 pays off: with no parliament, no free press, no legal politics, the novel became the only place the largest moral questions could be asked. Tolstoy writes War and Peace and Anna Karenina, then renounces rank, property, and the church, influencing a young lawyer named Gandhi. Dostoevsky comes back from his Siberian camp to write Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov. Chekhov, the grandson of a serf who bought his own freedom, reinvents the short story. The Mighty Handful build a Russian music against the conservatory-trained Tchaikovsky, whose 1812 Overture gives the West its image of Russia beating Napoleon. Mendeleev publishes the periodic table in 1869; Pavlov wins a Nobel Prize in 1904. The chapter's whole point is to hold both facts at once, the grandeur and the unfreedom, without letting either cancel the other.

takeaway: By the end you'll hold the empire's deepest contradiction without flinching, the greatest novels of the moral life produced by a state that never built a moral order.

bridge: So far the book has mostly told the story from St Petersburg, looking down, and even the Golden Age (Chapter 16) was the achievement of the Russian core. This chapter turns the empire inside out and looks at it from its edges, because the Russian Empire was never just Russians. By the 1897 census, of its roughly 125 million people only about 44 percent counted as Great Russians; it was a vast multi-ethnic patchwork, and the unfreedom at home had a second face in the millions of non-Russians the empire conquered without their consent.
setup: The chapter takes the directions in turn. South into the Caucasus, where Russia spent half a century in the Caucasian War, dated from around 1817 to 1864, producing the resistance leader Imam Shamil, who held the Muslim mountains for a quarter century before his 1859 capture, and the empire's single worst atrocity, the driving of the Circassians off their land into the sea in the 1860s, with deaths credibly in the hundreds of thousands, described by many as genocide. East into Central Asia, taking Tashkent in 1865, Khiva in 1873, and Merv in 1884, nearly fighting Britain at the 1885 Panjdeh incident. The empire even sells a piece of itself, Alaska, to the United States in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars, because land at the edge was negotiable when central power never was. The Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891 and running about 5,700 miles, is the physical answer to the size that opened the book. And the policy of russification, plus the Pale of Settlement and the post-1881 pogroms, manufactures by deliberate design some of the empire's most determined enemies. The question is how the empire of all the Russias made the people who would help light the powder.

bridge: The People's Will killed Alexander II on 1 March 1881 (Chapter 15) expecting the revolution. What they got was his son, Alexander III, who spent thirteen years destroying as much of his murdered father's reform as he could reach, on the theory that liberating anything had been the mistake. This chapter is the regime's clearest answer, after Nicholas I, to the question the book keeps asking: shown that the system is failing, will you change it or harden it? Alexander III hardens it, with a competence that makes him the most successful reactionary in the book.
setup: The mind of the reaction is Pobedonostsev, the chief ideologue who called democracy the great lie of our time and drafted the manifesto burying the near-constitution his father had approved. The Counter-Reforms narrow the zemstvo franchise, put a land captain back over the peasants, crush university autonomy, and build the highly effective Okhrana, the lineal heir of the Third Section. By the standard of holding the political surface still, it works. And then the regime does the thing that makes all the strangling beside the point: out of strategic necessity it force-marches Russia into the industrial revolution. Sergei Witte's program puts Russia on the gold standard in 1897 and, financed by French and Belgian capital, builds heavy industry and the Trans-Siberian, and the Baku oil fields briefly make the empire the world's largest oil producer. The detonator is that Witte builds an urban proletariat with no unions and no voice while Pobedonostsev guarantees it has no legal way to express a single demand. The Great Famine of 1891-1892 drives the intelligentsia decisively into opposition; Marxism arrives via Plekhanov; and the RSDLP's 1903 split creates Lenin's Bolsheviks. The question is what that compound, repression on top, capitalism underneath, ignites.

bridge: Alexander III (Chapter 18) died in 1894 leaving his counter-reformation looking like a complete success, the autocracy solid, the press silenced, the revolutionaries in exile, the economy booming, but underneath he had built a working class with no voice and let his enemies organize abroad. He left all of it, the booming furnaces, the frozen politics, the buried fuse, to a son utterly unequipped for any of it. His name was Nicholas, and he believed God had personally entrusted him with unlimited power to hand undiminished to his own son.
setup: Nicholas II is the most consequential incompetent in the book, a sincere, gentle, dutiful man of limited imagination applying the answer his father gave, hold and harden, to a country the railways and factories had made completely unlike the one Alexander III ruled. The omens come early: a crowd crush at Khodynka kills over a thousand at his 1896 coronation, and he attends a ball that evening. Against Witte's advice he pushes into the Far East, straight into Japan, which had done in forty years the institutional and industrial modernization Russia refused. The Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905 delivers the Crimean lesson again, harder: Japan takes Port Arthur, wins at Mukden, and annihilates the Baltic Fleet at Tsushima. Then, on 9 January 1905, troops fire on Father Gapon's peaceful petition march to the Winter Palace, and Bloody Sunday kills the sacred myth of the tsar-father that had held the unfreedom together since before Peter. The Revolution of 1905 forces the October Manifesto and a State Duma, a parliament six hundred years after England. The question is whether the regime, having survived 1905 just well enough, learns anything from it.

bridge: Chapter 19 left the regime having survived the dress rehearsal of 1905 and learned nothing from it, hollowing out the Duma it had been forced to grant and resting the dynasty's survival on the heir's secret hemophilia and a mystic's sway over a frightened empress. In 1913 it staged the magnificent Romanov Tercentenary, grandeur performing confidence over a state with a hollow center. Eighteen months away was the war that would end it. This is the chapter the entire book has been a fuse toward.
setup: A regime that survived for two and a third centuries takes six weeks in 1917 to disintegrate, because the First World War applies an unbearable load to a structure with the fatal flaw still in it. Russia enters the war in August 1914 and renames its capital Petrograd; the 1914 Battle of Tannenberg destroys an entire army, and General Samsonov shoots himself rather than report the scale. The 1916 Brusilov offensive shows the army can still fight superbly when led, bleeding it white for gains the system cannot exploit. Nicholas II takes personal command in 1915, welding his sacred person to every defeat and leaving the capital to the empress and Rasputin, whom aristocrats murder in December 1916, concluding the dynasty is destroying itself. Then the February Revolution begins as a bread queue and a strike, and ends when the Petrograd garrison refuses to fire and joins the crowd. On 2 March 1917, in a railway carriage at Pskov, Nicholas II signs his abdication for himself and his son, ending the Romanov dynasty after three hundred years. The question the chapter answers is why, when the moment came, almost no one was willing to fight to keep a tsar on the throne.
